nameStory: "Groundsel" comes from the Old English "grundeswelge," meaning "ground swallower" – a perfect description of how this little plant spreads rapidly across disturbed ground! The alternate name "old-man-in-the-spring" refers to the fluffy white seed heads that develop after flowering, resembling wispy old man's whiskers dancing in the breeze.
description: Common groundsel is a small, weedy annual herb that most people overlook in their gardens and sidewalk cracks. This unassuming plant grows 6-18 inches tall with deeply lobed, somewhat succulent leaves and clusters of tiny yellow flowers that look like miniature dandelions without the white petals. It's one of those "weeds" that's actually quite fascinating once you take a closer look – blooming nearly year-round and producing those distinctive fluffy seed heads that kids love to blow apart.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flower heads (about pencil-eraser sized) that look like dandelions missing their white ray petals – just the yellow center disc remains, clustered together at stem tips

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed, somewhat fleshy leaves that feel slightly succulent when pinched; lower leaves are more deeply cut while upper ones clasp the stem

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white puffball seed heads that appear quickly after flowering – each tiny seed has its own parachute of silky white hairs

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that forms small colonies in disturbed areas; stems are hollow, somewhat succulent, and branch near the top

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels slightly sticky and has a distinctive musty, somewhat unpleasant smell when crushed

habitat: Common groundsel thrives in disturbed, nutrient-rich soils throughout New England – look for it in gardens, vacant lots, roadsides, and anywhere the ground has been recently turned over. It particularly loves areas with loose, well-drained soil and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy companions like chickweed and plantain.

seasonality.spring: New plants emerge early and begin blooming by late spring, with fresh green foliage and the first clusters of yellow flowers appearing.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant yellow flower heads quickly followed by the characteristic white fluffy seed heads that disperse on summer breezes.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into fall in milder areas, with new generations of plants sprouting from summer-dispersed seeds.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back with hard frost, but in protected areas or mild winters, some individuals may persist and even continue flowering sporadically.

funFact: Common groundsel can complete its entire life cycle – from seed to flowering to seed production – in just 5-6 weeks, which means you might see up to 4 different generations blooming in a single growing season in the same spot!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with young dandelion plants, but groundsel's flowers lack the white ray petals (the "daisy petals") that dandelions have – they're just yellow centers. Memory trick: groundsel flowers look "incomplete" compared to dandelions, as if someone plucked all the white petals off!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being considered a garden weed, groundsel is actually an important early-season food source for beneficial insects when few other flowers are available, though it contains alkaloids that make it toxic to livestock and humans if consumed.
compareHints: Common groundsel differs from its relative sticky groundsel by being much less sticky to the touch and lacking the strong, unpleasant odor of its cousin. While sticky groundsel feels noticeably tacky when touched and smells quite rank, common groundsel is only slightly sticky and has a milder scent. Common groundsel also tends to be smaller overall and more widespread in disturbed urban areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sticky groundsel differs from its relative common groundsel by having the distinctive glandular-sticky coating and strong odor that common groundsel lacks.
